t.1.66.1: Having heard the words of Janaka, the great sage Viśvāmitra said to the king, "Show the bow to Rāma."
t.1.66.2: Then King Janaka commanded his ministers: "Let the divine bow, adorned with perfumes and garlands, be brought here."
t.1.66.3: Commanded by Janaka, the ministers entered the city, and at the king's order they came out again, placing that bow before them.
t.1.66.4: Fifty hundred tall and mighty men somehow hauled that eight-wheeled chest along.
t.1.66.7: Having heard their words, the king, with hands joined in reverence, addressed the great-souled Viśvāmitra and both of them, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
t.1.66.5: Taking charge of that approaching chest in which the bow lay, the king's ministers spoke to Janaka, who was like a god.
t.1.66.8: This excellent bow, O brahman, has been worshipped by the Janakas, and even kings of great valor were then unable to draw it.
t.1.66.9: Not all the hosts of the gods, nor the Asuras, nor the Rākṣasas, nor the foremost of the Gandharvas and Yakṣas, together with the Kiṃnaras and the great serpents, could accomplish this.
t.1.66.6: O King, lord of Mithilā, chief among kings, this excellent bow, honored by all kings, should be shown, if you wish.
t.1.66.10: What power, then, could mere men have to draw this bow, to string it, to fit an arrow to it, to shake it, or even to lift it?
t.1.66.11: Here then is that bow, the best of bows, which has been brought, O bull among sages; show it, O illustrious one, to these two princes.
t.1.66.12: But the righteous-souled Viśvāmitra, having heard what Janaka had said, spoke to Rāghava: "Rāma, my child, look at the bow!"
t.1.66.13: At the word of the great sage, Rāma opened the chest in which that bow lay, and having beheld the bow, he then spoke.
t.1.66.14: O brahman, I shall touch this excellent bow here with my hand, and I shall make the effort to lift it or even to string it.
t.1.66.16: While many thousands of men looked on, that righteous-souled Raghunandana strung the bow as if in play.
t.1.66.15: "Very well," the king and the sage said to him. At the sage's word, he grasped the bow by its middle with playful ease.
t.1.66.17: Having strung the bowstring, the mighty one drew it to its full stretch; and that best of men, of great renown, broke the bow in the middle.
t.1.66.18: From it there arose a great sound, resounding like a thunderclap, and a very great quaking of the earth, as of a mountain being split asunder.
t.1.66.19: And everywhere the men fell down, stupefied by that sound, all except the best of sages, the king, and the two Rāghavas.
t.1.66.21: O blessed one, I have witnessed the valour of Rāma, the son of Daśaratha. This is most wondrous and inconceivable, and it was never imagined by me.
t.1.66.20: When those people had recovered, the king, his fear gone, joined his palms and, skilled in speech, addressed these words to the bull among sages.
t.1.66.22: My daughter Sītā, having obtained as her husband Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, will bring glory to the family of the Janakas.
t.1.66.23: And my vow that she would be won by valour has come true, O Kauśika; Sītā, my daughter, dearer to me than life itself, is to be given to Rāma.
t.1.66.24: With your consent, O brahmin, let my ministers go swiftly and in haste by chariot to Ayodhyā. O Kauśika, may good fortune be with you!
t.1.66.26: Let them tell the king that the two Kākutsthas are under the protection of the sage, and let the very swift messengers bring the king, gladdened by the news, here.
t.1.66.25: With courteous words let them bring the king to my city, and let them proclaim on every side the giving of my daughter, for whom valor is the bride-price.
t.1.66.27: Kauśika said, “So be it,” and the righteous-souled king, having addressed his ministers, sent them to Ayodhyā in accordance with the command.
